## Abstract

Industry relies heavily on costly noble metals for use in pharmaceutical, agrochemical and

petroleum research. However, extraction of polymetallic ore deposits contributes to human rights

violations and irreversible ecological damage. These concerns must weigh on the scientific

community as rare-Earth feedstocks decline, and industrial means of satisfying demand grow more

extreme. By contrast, metal-free main group elements exhibit considerable natural abundance and

structural diversity, yet their use as catalysts remains underdeveloped. Chapter 1 discusses the

development of novel carbon-based bipyridinium and phenanthrolinium dications. Applicability

of these species towards catalytic hydrodefluorination (HDF) is reported in Chapter 2. Chapter 3

details the computations used to determine the Hydride Ion Affinity (HIA) of these species and to

examine their participation in HDF. Overall, this thesis demonstrates application of novel main

group initiators towards modes of reactivity potentially useful in the remediation of chemically

persistent perfluorinated compounds.

## Chapter 1 Development of Carbon Lewis Acids

### 1.1 Introduction

Lewis acids were first conceptualized by Gilbert N. Lewis in 1923 as a means of

delineating the behavior of molecules bearing electron deficiency.1 Continual advances in

synthetic chemistry have since furnished a diverse array of molecules categorizable under this

definition. Specifically, interest in novel main group (i.e. s- and p-block elements) systems has

furnished Lewis acids with a broad array of electronic, steric and stereochemical characteristics.2–

5 Consequent expansion to the understanding of bond connectivity, multidentate ligand

incorporation, and use of weakly coordinating counterions has arisen from the structural analysis

of novel inorganic coordination complexes.6 Moreover, incorporation of these tunable attributes

enables design of electrophilic cationic systems for use in chemical transformations, thus

imparting greater utility to these efforts.7 Each of these factors has contributed to development of

the novel model systems reported in this thesis.

Chapter 1 is organized as follows. First, the analysis of boron- and carbon- based Lewis acids will

be presented alongside discussion of the model for calculating Hydride Ion Affinity (HIA)

Ingleson and co-workers.8,9 This is relevant to understanding subsequent chapters. Next, analysis

of phosphorus-based dication predecessors will be undertaken, due to their role as conceptual

inspiration for the thesis work detailed herein. Accordingly, the final subsection reports the

development of novel bipyridinium and phenanthrolinium Lewis acids central to this thesis.

### 1.2 Analysis of Relevant Boron and Carbon Lewis Acids

The first preparation of tris(pentafluorophenyl)boron (BCF) was reported by Massey et al.

in 1963.10 As an expansion on classical trihaloborane BX3 (X= H, F, Cl, Br, I) Lewis acids, the

development of perfluoroaryl species neatly sidestepped degradation processes observed in their

perfluoroalkyl borane predecessors.11 In 1994, Yang et al. employed BCF as the co-catalyst in

formulation of zirconium-based Ziegler-Natta-type complexes (i.e. [L2ZrMe][MeB(C6F5)3]) for

use in olefin polymerization.12 By exposing the active site of Group 4 dialkyl-metallocene

derivatives, BCF facilitated isolation of a readily characterizable product. Subsequently, the high

impact and potential industrial utility behind these findings stimulated research into the

applications of electrophilic perfluoroaryl boranes.13 In 2006, formally unprecedented progress

into the development of metal-free hydrogenation systems was enabled via discovery of Frustrated

Lewis Pairs (FLPs) (Scheme 1a).14 In the 2007 follow up work, the unquenched reactivity of a

highly sterically encumbered Lewis basic phosphine (PtBu3) and Lewis acidic borane (BCF) was

used to preclude classical adduct formation, thus promoting metal-free activation of small

molecules (i.e. H2, CO, CO2, etc.).1,14 Inspired by its participation as the highly electron-deficient

electrophilic component in FLP-mediated heterolytic cleavage of H2, BCF swiftly garnered

attention for its ability to participate in a range of E-H σ-bond activation events (i.e. E = Si, B,

N).15–18

Elaboration on the use of borane electrophiles in cooperative Lewis acid/base catalysis has been

reported by Fontaine, Ingleson, Tamm, and Stephan, among many others.19,20 Notably, in 2008,

Tamm and co-workers established bifunctional cooperativity between BCF and the nucleophilic

1,3-di-tert-butylimidazol-2-ylidene N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) to achieve a novel carbene-

borane FLP, and therein effect activation of dihydrogen (Scheme 1b). In retrospect, this reactivity

is perhaps unsurprising, given the thermodynamic feasibility of effecting activation of H2 via

strongly Lewis acidic and basic components. Once sufficient steric encumbrance is incorporated

to prevent quenching pathways, there must simply exist a minimum threshold of cooperative

Lewis acid/base strength to achieve heterolytic cleavage.21 Consequently, effective prediction of

reactivity relies on determining this minimum value and tuning the catalytic system accordingly.22

As heterolytic H2 activation relies on hydride abstraction by the Lewis acid, it follows that

calculation of the Hydride Ion Affinity (HIA) of the Lewis acid could provide insight into its

potential reactivity; further, a sufficiently strong Lewis acid could compensate for a weaker Lewis

base.22,23 Continuing this line of reasoning, Ingleson and co-workers performed DFT

computations at the M06-2X/6-11G(d,p) level of theory to determine the HIA of catechol and

thiocatechol ligated borenium cations (i.e. three-coordinate borocations).9 These computations

enabled Ingleson and co-workers to formulate a reactivity series of borenium cations towards

participation in ionic hydrogenation and informed our own calculations (see Chapter 3). As a

result, it was concluded that use of weak π-donor ligands (e.g., Cl- and Ph-) increased the HIA of

borenium complexes, thereby facilitating successful FLP-type activation of deuterium gas (D2) in

the presence of a lutidine-based ligand (Scheme 2a).9 This work was followed by report of an

acridine-stabilized borenium species (i.e. three-coordinate borocation), capable of activating D2

in the presence of a relatively weak 2,4,6-tri-tert-butylpyridine base (Scheme 2b).8

In 2014, Ingleson and co-workers further advanced this research by developing N-

methylacridinium salts, capable of σ-bond activation via hydride abstraction.24 However, these

carbon-based Lewis acids also succeeded in transferring the hydride to an acceptor substrate,

thereby showcasing useful reductive reactivity (Scheme 3a).24 The significance of these findings

is emphasized by comparison with literature precedent. Previous reports by Arduengo et al. had

established the efficacy of trityl salts towards cooperative small molecule activation (Scheme

3b).25 Critically, these carbon-centered electrophiles exhibit HIA’s high enough to establish

hydride abstraction, yet are incapable of performing subsequent hydride transfer. The HIA of these

species differ drastically, indicating that a key determinant in reactivity is controlling HIA

(Scheme 3c). Thus, Ingleson and co-workers successfully furthered the conceptualization of HIA

as a tunable characteristic, directly relatable to catalytic reactivity.8

### 1.3 Development of novel carbon-based Lewis acids

As early as 1975, Sullivan et al. reported using dibromoethane to quaternize bipyridine scaffolds;

these efforts furnished the target diquat dibromide salts under benchtop conditions.31 Accordingly,

suitable crystals for X-ray diffraction analysis were prepared. Structural analysis reported that

protons on the ethylene bridge exhibit pseudoaxial and pseudoequatorial orientations, while

considerable rotational and inversion barriers were also found.31 Accordingly, this preparation was

adapted to furnish the desired bromide salts from neutral bipyridine and  phenanthroline starting

materials, thereby furnishing 1 to 3 and 7 to 8, respectively (Scheme 6).

Intermediates were washed in reaction grade acetone and hexanes to remove trace impurities and

any unreacted starting materials. Following this step, each bromide species was used to synthesize

both the corresponding triflate ([CF3SO3]-, i.e., [OTf]-) and tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)borate

Scheme 6. Preparation of carbon-based dications


<!-- Page 22 -->


9

([B(C6F5)4]-) salts. In preparation of the former, transformations using trimethylsilyl

trifluoromethanesulfonate (TMSOTf) were used to furnish the triflate salts of each species, using

acetonitrile as reaction media. Following reaction progress, all volatiles were removed in vacuo

and the product subsequently wash with diethyl ether. It is notable how robust these Lewis acidic

species were in the presence of coordinating solvents. The lack of solvent coordination with the

carbon-centered Lewis acids indicates excellent compatibility in a range of solvent systems.

Preparation of the tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)borate salts was undertaken for their subsequent use

in reactivity studies. This was accomplished by reacting the bromide precursors with trityl

tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)borate ([CPh3][B(C6F5)4]) in non-coordinating arene solvent (i.e.

fluorobenzene or ortho-difluorobenzene (ODFB)) to prevent unproductive coordination to the

trityl carbocation center (Scheme 6). As an exception, the corresponding tert-Butyl substituted

bipyridinium tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)borate salt was prepared using 1.90 equivalents of

freshly prepared silylium tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)borate in fluorobenzene. This synthesis was

carried out following protocol reported by Chitnis et al.28 All products were subsequently

extracted into acetonitrile, filtered over a short celite plug, and evaporated in vacuo. Oils were

subsequently triturated using pentanes and isolated as the corresponding powder. Further,

products underwent thorough drying by vacuum to remove any residual solvent. Due to solubility,

CD3CN proved most effective for characterization. However, the more expensive alternative

CD2Cl2 is expected to be equally compatible. For full experimental details, see Chapter 4.

To the best of our knowledge, this work describes the first known isolation of these triflate and

tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)borate complexes.32 Further, the novelty of applying these carbon-

based dications towards main group synthesis was pursued as a method to continue a line of

### 2.1   Introduction

Innovation in chemical research must adapt to satisfy present and emerging demands.

Currently, we face mounting pressure to address a rapidly warming global atmosphere, arising in

part from global emissions of hydrofluorocarbons (HFC’s).33 HFC’s exhibit long atmospheric

lifetimes and a disproportionately high global warming potential (GWP).34 Certain persistent

perfluorinated chemicals have been proven to exhibit per molecule infrared-radiation (IR)

persistence of HFC’s is largely derived from their fluorine atom(s), yet cleavage of the highly

Considerable advances in the area of transition metal-mediated C-F bond activation have resulted

in diversification of hydrodefluorination (HDF) methodology to replace a fluoride residue with a

hydride.38–42 These systems successfully demonstrate HDF of polyfluorinated compounds; this

may enable new avenues of potentially remediating environmentally persistent species. However,

these protocols inherently produce toxic metal byproducts and demand wasteful chromatographic

purification methods.39,40,42

The work reported herein demonstrates utility of novel carbon-based phenanthrolinium dications

The proposed catalytic cycle presents two potential outcomes; however, both follow the same

preliminary steps. First, the dicationic Lewis acid (I) abstracts a hydride ion from triethylsilane,

### 3.1 Hydride Ion Affinities

Characterization of Lewis acidity can be accomplished using a variety of methods.

Classically, the Guttman-Beckett method has offered a robust means of evaluating the Lewis

acidity of main group, organic, and organometallic compounds.59 This method employs the

phosphoryl functionality in triethylphosphine oxide to coordinate with the target Lewis acid, with

the corresponding 31P NMR shift used to determine Lewis acid strength.60 This approach is

attractive, as the 31P nucleus is 100% naturally abundant and exhibits good analytical sensitivity.61

By comparison, measurement of Fluoride Ion Affinity (FIA) uses computational methods to

determine a complex’s ability to accept a fluoride (F-) anion.62

Furthermore, considerable discussion has already been presented on the significance of evaluating

Hydride Ion Affinity (HIA) in the context of novel main group complexes. Intuitively, HIA

provides a method of assessing a Lewis acid’s ability to participate in hydride ion abstraction.

This metric is valuable in the context of silylium-mediated catalysis, wherein cleavage of a σ(Si-

H) bond initiates the catalytic cycle. Determination of HIA for all experimentally investigated

species was therefore pursued. The HIA of the tetramethyl substituted phenanthrolinium salt was

not undertaken. Additional calculations were performed for additional complexes, the synthesis

of which was not pursued. This was done in an effort to contrast the nature of this work with

previous studies and provide further insight into reactivity of this class of carbon Lewis acids.

All HIA values were undertaken using the Gaussian 09 software program and were submitted to

the Compute Canada cluster. Calculations were exclusively performed at the M06-2X/6-
